lessons.title: Lab: The standard atmosphere

story.title: Why Leh is hard on engines

scenes.text: A pilot flying into Leh (3,256 m) is told her take-off roll will be much longer than at Delhi.
The reason is air density. To compare flights anywhere, engineers use one reference atmosphere.

steps.title: ISA definition
steps.body:
The **International Standard Atmosphere (ISA)** fixes sea-level values: T0 = 288.15 K, p0 = 101,325 Pa, ρ0 = 1.225 kg/m³, a0 = 340.3 m/s, and a lapse rate **L = −6.5 K per km** in the troposphere (0–11 km). From 11 to 20 km the temperature is constant at 216.65 K (isothermal layer).

Assumptions: dry air, perfect gas p = ρRT with R = 287.05 J/(kg·K), and hydrostatic equilibrium dp = −ρ g dh.

steps.title: Derivation of the troposphere formulas
steps.body:
Hydrostatic: dp = −ρg dh. Gas law: ρ = p/(RT). Combine: dp/p = −(g/RT) dh. With T = T0 + L h (L = −0.0065 K/m), dh = dT/L, so dp/p = −(g/(R L)) dT/T. Integrating:

**p/p0 = (T/T0)^(−g/(R L))** with −g/(RL) = 9.80665/(287.05×0.0065) = **5.2559**.

Since ρ ∝ p/T: **ρ/ρ0 = (T/T0)^4.2559**.

In the isothermal layer: p = p11 · exp(−g(h−11000)/(R·216.65)).

steps.title: Solved example: pressure, density and geopotential altitude
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C instead of kelvin in (T/T0).
- Applying the troposphere formula above 11 km (the stratosphere is isothermal).
- Confusing pressure altitude, density altitude and geometric altitude. Density altitude is the ISA altitude that has the same density as the actual air; hot days at Leh give a high density altitude and poor performance.

lessons.title: Fluid properties, viscosity and dimensionless numbers

story.title: Honey, water and a wind tunnel

scenes.text: Honey flows slowly because its viscosity is huge; air barely resists shear, yet this tiny viscosity creates drag on every aircraft.
To test a 1:10 model in a tunnel, engineers match non-dimensional numbers rather than sizes.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
- **Density ρ** (kg/m³) and **pressure p** (Pa).
- **Dynamic viscosity μ** (Pa·s). Newton's law: **τ = μ du/dy**. Air at 15 °C: μ = 1.789×10⁻⁵ Pa·s. Kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ = 1.46×10⁻⁵ m²/s.
- Viscosity of gases *rises* with temperature (Sutherland's law); of liquids it falls.
- **Speed of sound a = √(γRT)**; 340.3 m/s at 288.15 K.
- Compressibility: for a gas, ρ changes with p; incompressible flow is a good model when M < 0.3 (density change < ~5%).

steps.title: Key dimensionless numbers
steps.body:
- **Reynolds number Re = ρVL/μ** — inertial/viscous forces; governs boundary-layer behaviour.
- **Mach number M = V/a** — compressibility.
- **Pressure coefficient Cp = (p − p∞)/q∞**, **q∞ = ½ρ∞V∞²**.
- Lift/drag coefficients CL = L/(q S), CD = D/(q S).

Buckingham π: with n variables and k fundamental dimensions you get n − k independent groups. For drag D = f(ρ, V, L, μ, a): 6 variables, 3 dimensions (M, L, T) → 3 groups: CD, Re, M.

steps.title: Solved example: Reynolds number of a trainer wing
steps.body:
Chord 1.5 m, V = 50 m/s, sea level (ρ = 1.225, μ = 1.789×10⁻⁵).
Re = 1.225×50×1.5/1.789×10⁻⁵ = 91.875/1.789×10⁻⁵ = **5.14×10⁶**.
Transition from laminar to turbulent on a flat plate occurs near Re_x ≈ 5×10⁵, so the wing is mostly turbulent.

steps.title: Solved example: shear stress and similarity
steps.body:
(a) Velocity gradient at the wall of du/dy = 2,000 s⁻¹: τ = 1.789×10⁻⁵×2000 = 0.0358 Pa.
(b) A 1/10-scale model is tested in the same air at the same Mach number: to match Re you need V_model = 10 V_full. For a full-scale 60 m/s that is 600 m/s, which breaks the Mach match. This is why pressurised or cryogenic tunnels exist: raising ρ (or lowering T to reduce μ/ρ) restores Re without raising speed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using chord for Re when the problem gives distance x from the leading edge (local Re_x).
- Forgetting that μ depends on temperature, not pressure (to first order).
- Treating M < 0.3 as an exact boundary; it is a rule of thumb.

lessons.title: Lab: Continuity, Bernoulli and the wind-tunnel contraction

scenes.text: A student team builds a low-speed open-circuit tunnel for a university lab.
The contraction squeezes air from a 2.0 m² inlet to a 0.5 m² test section. They need the pressure drop to size the fan.

steps.title: Continuity and Bernoulli
steps.body:
Steady incompressible flow in a stream tube: **A1V1 = A2V2** (mass: ρAV = const.).

Along a streamline of steady, inviscid, incompressible flow with negligible body force: **p + ½ρV² = p0** (total/stagnation pressure). Derivation: Euler's equation along s: V dV/ds = −(1/ρ) dp/ds; integrate with ρ = const.

Bernoulli does *not* apply across a fan/pump (energy added), through shocks, or in strongly viscous regions.

steps.title: Solved example: tunnel contraction
steps.body:
A1 = 2.0 m², A2 = 0.5 m², V2 = 50 m/s, ρ = 1.225.
1. V1 = V2 A2/A1 = 50×0.5/2.0 = 12.5 m/s.
2. Δp = p1 − p2 = ½ρ(V2² − V1²) = 0.5×1.225×(2500 − 156.25) = 0.6125×2343.75 = **1,435.5 Pa**.
3. Contraction ratio 4; this small Δp is why tunnel manometers read in mm of water (1,435 Pa ≈ 146 mm H₂O).

steps.title: Solved example: pitot-static airspeed
steps.body:
A pitot tube measures p0 − p = 1,500 Pa at sea level. Since p0 − p = ½ρV²:
V = √(2×1500/1.225) = √2448.98 = **49.5 m/s**.
The static port gives p; the pitot port gives p0; an air-speed indicator is a differential gauge calibrated at sea-level density.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Bernoulli between points on different streamlines when total pressure differs (e.g. in a wake or boundary layer).
- Using gauge/absolute pressures inconsistently.
- Using Bernoulli through a propeller or fan disc.

lessons.title: Lab: Pressure coefficient and stagnation points

scenes.text: A wind-tunnel report gives pressure coefficients along an airfoil. A negative Cp means suction.
You must check whether the numbers make physical sense.

steps.title: Cp definition
steps.body:
**Cp = (p − p∞)/q∞ = 1 − (V/V∞)²** (incompressible). At a stagnation point V = 0 so **Cp = +1** (the maximum possible). Where local speed exceeds free stream, Cp < 0 (suction). The minimum Cp on a wing marks the suction peak; if Cp falls below the vapour/cavitation limit or if M_local reaches 1, other physics intervene.

Lift from pressure data: cn = ∮(Cp_lower − Cp_upper) d(x/c), then cl ≈ cn cosα (small angle: cl ≈ cn).

steps.title: Solved example: lift from a simple Cp distribution
steps.body: A flat-plate-like section has Cp_upper = −0.6 and Cp_lower = +0.2, constant over the chord. cn = ∫(0.2 − (−0.6)) dx/c = 0.8. At small α: cl ≈ 0.8. With q∞ = 2,205 Pa and chord 1 m, lift per metre span = 0.8×2205×1 = 1,764 N/m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Plotting Cp upward positive; aerodynamicists conventionally plot **−Cp** upward so that the upper surface appears on top.
- Sign errors: lower surface at positive Cp pushes the wing up.
- Forgetting that Cp > 1 is impossible in incompressible flow.

story.title: Why the ASI lies at altitude

scenes.text: A Cessna cruises at 3,000 m. The airspeed indicator shows 60 m/s, but the GPS ground speed in still air is higher.
You reconcile the numbers using density ratio σ.

steps.title: Airspeed definitions
steps.body:
- **IAS**: raw instrument reading.
- **CAS**: IAS corrected for instrument and position error.
- **EAS**: CAS corrected for compressibility; at low speed EAS ≈ CAS. It satisfies ½ρ0 V_EAS² = ½ρ V_TAS² = q.
- **TAS**: the true speed through the air. **TAS = EAS/√σ**, σ = ρ/ρ0.

The instrument senses dynamic pressure q only, so it reads as if at sea-level density.

steps.title: Solved example: dynamic pressure is the same
steps.body: q = ½×1.225×60² = 2,205 Pa (what the instrument senses). Check: ½×0.9093×69.64² = 0.45465×4849.7 = 2,205 Pa ✓. The wing 'feels' the same dynamic pressure, so the same lift at the same CL even though TAS is higher; the stall *EAS* is constant with altitude, while stall TAS rises.

steps.title: Wind triangle
steps.body: Ground speed = TAS vector + wind vector. A 10 m/s headwind reduces ground speed to 59.6 m/s here.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using σ instead of √σ.
- Assuming the ASI reading changes with altitude at the same TAS: it falls.
- Applying EAS/TAS conversion without compressibility correction at M > 0.3.

lessons.title: Stream function, velocity potential and circulation

scenes.text: A CFD engineer sketches streamlines before running a solver; the lines must obey mass conservation.
Two scalar functions describe the whole 2-D incompressible irrotational flow field.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
**Stream function ψ(x,y)** (2-D incompressible): u = ∂ψ/∂y, v = −∂ψ/∂x. It satisfies continuity automatically; ψ = constant lines are streamlines; the difference Δψ between two streamlines is the volume flow rate per unit span.

**Velocity potential φ** (irrotational flow, ∇×V = 0): V = ∇φ, so u = ∂φ/∂x, v = ∂φ/∂y. Incompressibility ∇·V = 0 gives **Laplace's equation ∇²φ = 0** (and ∇²ψ = 0). Equipotential lines (φ = const) are orthogonal to streamlines.

**Circulation Γ = −∮V·ds** (sign conventions vary; here counter-clockwise is positive with Γ = −∮ for clockwise-positive aerodynamic convention). By Stokes' theorem Γ = ∬ω dA, so irrotational flow has Γ = 0 around any closed curve not enclosing a singularity.

steps.title: Why potential flow works
steps.body: Outside thin boundary layers and wakes, vorticity is negligible, so potential flow predicts pressure distribution and lift well. Because Laplace's equation is **linear**, solutions can be added (superposition): the foundation of panel methods. Pressure is found afterwards from Bernoulli.

steps.title: Solved example: uniform flow
steps.body: u = V∞ = 30 m/s, v = 0: ψ = V∞ y, φ = V∞ x. Between streamlines y = 0 and y = 0.5 m the flow rate per metre span = Δψ = 30×0.5 = **15 m²/s**.

steps.title: Solved example: check a given field
steps.body: Given u = 2x, v = −2y. Continuity: ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 2 − 2 = 0 ✓. Vorticity ω = ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y = 0 ✓ (irrotational). φ = x² − y², ψ = 2xy. This is stagnation-point flow.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing the sign convention of ψ (u = ∂ψ/∂y).
- Assuming φ exists for rotational flow.
- Forgetting that ψ exists for any 2-D incompressible flow, but φ only for irrotational flow.

lessons.title: Lab: Source, sink, vortex and doublet

scenes.text: A panel-method program places small sources and vortices on the surface of a wing.
You learn the velocity fields of the basic bricks.

steps.title: Elementary flows (polar coordinates)
steps.body:
- **Source of strength Λ (m²/s)**: V_r = Λ/(2πr), V_θ = 0; φ = (Λ/2π) ln r; ψ = (Λ/2π) θ. Λ < 0 is a sink.
- **Free (irrotational) vortex of strength Γ**: V_θ = Γ/(2πr) (counter-clockwise positive), V_r = 0; φ = (Γ/2π)θ; ψ = −(Γ/2π) ln r. Singular at r = 0, circulation Γ around it, irrotational elsewhere.
- **Doublet of strength κ**: a source and sink of equal strength brought together (Λ·2a = κ constant): ψ = −κ sinθ/(2πr), V_r = −(κ/(2πr²)) cosθ, V_θ = −(κ/(2πr²)) sinθ.
- **Uniform stream**: V∞ in +x: ψ = V∞ r sinθ.

steps.title: Solved example: source
steps.body: Λ = 10 m²/s at r = 2 m: V_r = 10/(2π×2) = 0.796 m/s. Using Bernoulli with p∞ = 101,325 Pa at infinity (V = 0): p = p∞ − ½ρV² = 101,325 − 0.5×1.225×0.633 = 101,324.6 Pa.

steps.title: Solved example: vortex
steps.body: Γ = 20 m²/s, r = 1.5 m: V_θ = 20/(2π×1.5) = **2.122 m/s**. Doubling r halves V_θ (V ∝ 1/r). Compare a rigid-body vortex where V ∝ r; real vortices have a viscous core (Rankine vortex).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ψ = Γ/(2π) ln r without the minus sign.
- Treating a vortex as having zero circulation (the integral around the origin = Γ).
- Dividing by r instead of r² for the doublet.

story.title: The paradox of the smooth cylinder

scenes.text: A chimney in the wind: ideal-flow theory says it feels no drag at all.

steps.title: Superposition
steps.body:
Uniform flow + doublet: **ψ = V∞ r sinθ (1 − R²/r²)** with R² = κ/(2πV∞). The streamline ψ = 0 is the circle r = R, so it can be a solid cylinder.

Surface velocity: **V_θ = −2V∞ sinθ**. Maximum speed 2V∞ at θ = 90°. Stagnation points at θ = 0°, 180°.

**Cp = 1 − 4 sin²θ**. Cp = +1 at stagnation, −3 at the shoulders. The distribution is symmetric front/back, so net drag and net lift are both zero (**d'Alembert's paradox**).

lessons.title: Lab: Lifting cylinder and the Kutta–Joukowski theorem

scenes.text: A footballer bends a free kick: spin makes the ball experience a sideways force (Magnus effect).
The same circulation idea gives lift on a wing.

steps.title: Add a vortex
steps.body:
Adding a vortex of strength Γ at the origin keeps r = R a streamline:
**V_θ = −2V∞ sinθ − Γ/(2πR)** (clockwise Γ positive here). **Cp = 1 − (2 sinθ + Γ/(2πRV∞))²**.

Stagnation points: sinθ = −Γ/(4πRV∞). They merge at the bottom when Γ = 4πRV∞; beyond that they leave the surface.

**Kutta–Joukowski theorem**: **L′ = ρ∞ V∞ Γ** per unit span, perpendicular to V∞. It holds for any 2-D closed body, not only cylinders — the cornerstone of airfoil theory. Drag is still zero in ideal flow.

steps.title: Solved example: lift coefficient
steps.body: Based on frontal dimension 2R: cl = L′/(q∞·2R) = 441/(551.25×0.2) = 4.0, which equals Γ/(R V∞) = 12/3 = 4.0 ✓. (q∞ = 0.5×1.225×900 = 551.25 Pa.) The theoretical maximum cl = 4π when Γ = 4πRV∞.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that Γ is determined by the Kutta condition for airfoils; for a cylinder it is freely chosen (by spin).
- Using L = ρVΓ without the span.
- Giving the wrong direction: lift is perpendicular to V∞, rotated from the freestream opposite to the sense of circulation.

scenes.text: A naval architect wants to shape a mast's leading fairing from a source in a uniform flow.
You find where the stagnation point sits and how wide the body becomes.

steps.title: Source in a uniform stream
steps.body: ψ = V∞ r sinθ + (Λ/2π) θ. The dividing streamline ψ = Λ/2 passes through the stagnation point on the axis at **x = −b with b = Λ/(2πV∞)**. Far downstream the body approaches a total width **Λ/V∞** (half-width Λ/(2V∞)). The body is semi-infinite (open at the rear): a Rankine half-body. Adding an equal sink downstream closes it: the **Rankine oval**.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
V∞ = 20 m/s, Λ = 30 m²/s.
b = 30/(2π×20) = 0.2387 m.
Total asymptotic width = 30/20 = 1.5 m.

steps.title: Solved example: width at the source
steps.body: At θ = 90°, on the dividing streamline: V∞ r sinθ + (Λ/2π)(π/2) = Λ/2 ⇒ 20 r = 15 − 7.5 = 7.5 ⇒ r = 0.375 m, i.e. width 0.75 m directly above/below the source.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing the stagnation point downstream of the source.
- Using Λ/V∞ as the half-width (it is the full width).
- Forgetting that a half-body is open: use a source + sink for a closed shape.

lessons.title: Lab: Airfoil geometry, NACA codes and force coefficients

scenes.text: A student sees NACA 2412 on a model glider plan and wonders what the four digits encode.
The numbers give the shape directly, which is why the series is a universal language.

steps.title: Geometry terms
steps.body:
Chord c, mean camber line (midway between surfaces), thickness distribution, leading-edge radius, trailing-edge angle, angle of attack α (between chord and freestream).

**NACA 4-digit MPXX**: M = maximum camber in % chord; P = position of max camber in tenths of chord; XX = maximum thickness in % chord. So **NACA 2412**: 2% camber at 0.4c, 12% thick. **NACA 0012** is symmetric.

**5-digit** (e.g. 23012) designs the camber line for a given design cl; **6-series** (e.g. 63-212) is a laminar-flow family.

steps.title: Coefficients
steps.body:
Per unit span: **cl = l/(q c)**, **cd = d/(q c)**, **cm = m/(q c²)**, with nose-up moment positive. Section forces can be resolved normal/axial to the chord: **cl = cn cosα − ca sinα**, **cd = cn sinα + ca cosα**.

**Centre of pressure (xcp)**: the point where the moment is zero; it moves with α. **Aerodynamic centre (xac)**: moment is independent of α; about 0.25c in subsonic thin-airfoil theory. Moments transfer: **cm,le = cm,c/4 − cl/4** (small α).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing the aerodynamic centre with the centre of pressure.
- Using cm about the wrong reference point.
- Reading NACA 2412 as '24% camber'.

lessons.title: The Kutta condition, starting vortex and Kelvin's theorem

story.title: How an airfoil gets its circulation

scenes.text: As a wing starts moving from rest, a visible swirl forms at the trailing edge and is left behind.
That starting vortex carries opposite circulation to the one 'bound' to the wing.

steps.title: The problem
steps.body:
Potential flow around an airfoil allows infinitely many solutions (any Γ). Real flow picks one. **Kutta condition**: for a sharp trailing edge the flow leaves smoothly; the velocity there is finite and the upper and lower pressures are equal, so Γ is fixed. For a cusped TE the two surface speeds are equal and nonzero; for a finite-angle TE the TE is a stagnation point.

**Kelvin's circulation theorem**: for inviscid, barotropic flow with conservative body forces, circulation around a fluid loop is conserved (DΓ/Dt = 0). A wing starting from rest has total Γ = 0, so the starting vortex (−Γ) is shed as the bound vortex (+Γ) forms.

steps.title: Consequences
steps.body:
- Lift per span L′ = ρ V∞ Γ, with Γ set by the Kutta condition.
- With a changing α the wing sheds more vorticity (unsteady lift, Wagner function).
- The starting vortex stays near the take-off point: wake turbulence behind heavy aircraft descends from the tip vortices that link back to it.
- At stall, flow separates and the Kutta condition fails to hold in its simple form.

steps.title: Solved example: Γ from lift
steps.body: A 1.2 m chord airfoil at 40 m/s produces l′ = 1,046.6 N/m. Γ = L′/(ρV∞) = 1046.6/(1.225×40) = **21.36 m²/s**.

steps.title: Solved example: starting vortex
steps.body: The bound vortex has Γ = 21.36 m²/s anticlockwise-equivalent. Total circulation must remain zero, so the starting vortex has −21.36 m²/s. Its induced speed at r = 5 m is 21.36/(2π×5) = 0.68 m/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying that 'Kutta condition creates lift'; it only picks the unique Γ.
- Applying Kutta to a blunt trailing edge.
- Forgetting that the theorem is for inviscid flow; viscosity creates the starting vortex in reality.

scenes.text: Wind-tunnel data for a NACA 0012 shows cl climbing 0.11 per degree.
Theory predicts exactly that: 2π per radian = 0.1097 per degree.

steps.title: Model
steps.body:
Replace the airfoil by a **vortex sheet along the chord** with strength γ(x), satisfying the flow tangency on the camber line and the Kutta condition γ(c) = 0. For small α the boundary condition becomes

(1/2π) ∫₀^c γ(ξ) dξ/(x − ξ) = V∞ (α − dz/dx).

With the transformation x = (c/2)(1 − cosθ), γ(θ) = 2αV∞ (1 + cosθ)/sinθ for a symmetric (flat-plate) airfoil.

Results: **cl = 2πα**, **cm,le = −πα/2**, **cm,c/4 = 0**, and **xcp = xac = c/4**. Lift-curve slope a0 = 2π per radian = 0.1097 per degree. Valid for thin airfoils at small α (about < 10°) before viscous effects.

lessons.title: Lab: Cambered airfoils – α_L0 and cm,ac

scenes.text: A cambered wing already lifts when its chord is level with the wind.
The angle where lift vanishes is the zero-lift angle α_L0, negative for positive camber.

steps.title: Results
steps.body:
For camber line z(x), with x = (c/2)(1−cosθ): γ(θ) = 2V∞ [A0 (1+cosθ)/sinθ + Σ An sin(nθ)], where
**A0 = α − (1/π)∫₀^π (dz/dx) dθ**, **An = (2/π)∫₀^π (dz/dx) cos(nθ) dθ**.

**cl = 2π(α − α_L0)** where α_L0 = −(1/π)∫₀^π (dz/dx)(cosθ − 1) dθ.
**cm,c/4 = (π/4)(A2 − A1)** and cm,le = −(π/4)(2A0 + 2A1 − A2) so that cl = π(2A0 + A1).

The aerodynamic centre is at c/4: cm,c/4 is the constant cm,ac, and is negative for positive camber. Typical NACA 2412: α_L0 ≈ −2.1°, cm,ac ≈ −0.045.

steps.title: Solved example: required angle
steps.body: A cambered section with α_L0 = −2.1° needs cl = 0.9 for cruise: α = α_L0 + cl/(2π) = −2.1° + 0.9/6.2832 rad = −2.1° + 8.21° = **6.11°**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using α when you should use (α − α_L0).
- Believing thickness changes α_L0 much (to first order it does not; camber does).
- Missing the sign: positive camber → negative α_L0 → negative cm,ac.

scenes.text: A design team compares NACA 2412 and 0012 for a two-seat trainer wing.

steps.title: Real behaviour
steps.body:
- Lift curve is linear to α ≈ 10–12°, then rolls over at **cl,max** (NACA 2412: about 1.6 at α ≈ 16° at Re = 3×10⁶; NACA 0012: about 1.4–1.5 at 14–16°).
- **Stall types**: trailing-edge (thick sections, gentle), leading-edge (thin sections, abrupt), thin-airfoil (long bubble, gradual).
- Higher Reynolds number delays separation and raises cl,max.
- Cambered sections give higher cl,max and lower cruise drag at design cl; symmetric ones suit tail surfaces and aerobatic wings.
- Thicker sections (to ~15%) give more structure depth but higher drag.

lessons.title: Wing geometry, tip vortices and downwash

scenes.text: Migrating geese fly in a V to ride the upwash of the bird ahead: a living lesson in tip vortices.
Every finite wing sheds such vortices and pays a drag penalty for them.

steps.title: Geometry
steps.body:
- Span b, planform area S, **aspect ratio AR = b²/S** (= b/c for a rectangular wing).
- Root chord c_r, tip chord c_t, **taper ratio λ = c_t/c_r**; mean chord c̄ = S/b.
- **Mean aerodynamic chord (MAC)**: c̄_A = (2/S)∫₀^{b/2} c² dy; for a trapezoidal wing, MAC = (2/3) c_r (1 + λ + λ²)/(1 + λ).
- Sweep angle Λ (usually at quarter-chord), dihedral Γ, geometric twist (washout: tip incidence < root).

**Physical picture**: higher pressure on the lower surface and lower pressure on the upper surface leak around the tip, rolling up into two **trailing vortices**. They induce a downward velocity **w (downwash)** over the wing, tilting the local relative wind down by the **induced angle α_i**; the local lift tilts backward, giving **induced drag Di**.

steps.title: Solved example: why AR matters
steps.body: Same area S = 14.4 m²: a span of 8.5 m gives AR = 72.25/14.4 = 5.0, a span of 12 m gives AR = 10. Higher AR means a smaller fraction of the wing near the tips and weaker downwash, so lower induced drag (CDi ∝ 1/AR).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using AR = b/c̄ when the chord varies without defining c̄ = S/b.
- Placing the MAC at the root; it lies at spanwise station y = (b/6)(1+2λ)/(1+λ).
- Treating induced drag as friction: it is a pressure drag due to lift.

lessons.title: Lab: Lifting-line theory and elliptic loading

scenes.text: In 1918–19 Ludwig Prandtl proposed replacing each wing section by a bound vortex with a trailing vortex sheet.
The elliptic distribution turns out to be the most efficient: minimum induced drag for given lift and span.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body:
Replace the wing by a **lifting line**: circulation Γ(y) varies along the span; trailing vortices of strength dΓ = (dΓ/dy)dy are shed. Biot–Savart gives the downwash

**w(y0) = −(1/4π) ∫₋b/2^{b/2} (dΓ/dy) dy/(y0 − y)**, so **α_i(y0) = −w/V∞**.

Effective angle α_eff = α − α_i; local lift: Γ(y) = ½ a0 V∞ c(y)[α − α_L0 − α_i]. This is **Prandtl's integro-differential equation**.

**Elliptic loading**: Γ(y) = Γ0 √(1 − (2y/b)²). Then downwash is uniform: **w = −Γ0/(2b)**, so
- **α_i = CL/(π AR)**,
- **CDi = CL²/(π AR)** (the minimum for a planar wing),
- Γ0 = 2 V∞ S CL/(π b)  [from L = ρV∞Γ0 πb/4].
An untwisted elliptic planform gives elliptic loading (the Spitfire wing).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that α_i uses AR, not b/c.
- Using CDi = CL²/AR (missing π).
- Treating lifting-line theory as valid for low AR (< 4) or high sweep; use lifting-surface/vortex-lattice methods there.

story.title: Why a real wing is not elliptic

scenes.text: A rectangular wing is cheap to build but its load is not elliptic, so its induced drag is a bit higher.
We capture the penalty in a single factor e.

steps.title: Results for general wings
steps.body:
For arbitrary planform (Fourier series Γ = 2bV∞ Σ A_n sin nθ): **CL = π AR A1**, **CDi = (CL²/(π AR))(1 + δ)** with δ = Σ n (A_n/A_1)² (n ≥ 2) ≥ 0. Define the **span efficiency factor e = 1/(1 + δ)**:

**CDi = CL²/(π e AR)**; typical e: 0.95–1.0 for good tapered wings (λ ≈ 0.4), 0.85–0.9 for rectangular, 0.7–0.85 for whole aircraft ('Oswald efficiency').

**Finite-wing lift slope** (elliptic): **a = a0/(1 + a0/(π AR))**; general: **a = a0/(1 + (a0/(π AR))(1 + τ))** where τ ≈ 0.05–0.25. With CL = a(α − α_L0,wing): the induced angle subtracts from the effective angle, flattening the curve, and the zero-lift angle is unchanged.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a0 for a whole wing.
- Using e > 1 (impossible for planar wings).
- Forgetting that α_i is subtracted from the geometric angle to get the effective angle.

lessons.title: Twist, sweep, winglets and stall patterns

story.title: Why airliners bend their wingtips up

scenes.text: Look at a modern airliner: the tips sweep up into winglets, saving several percent fuel.
A lightly loaded tip would also keep the ailerons effective at stall.

steps.title: Design features
steps.body:
- **Washout** (tip at lower incidence) moves stall inboard, preserving aileron control; aerodynamic washout uses different airfoils.
- **Sweep** delays compressibility drag rise (Unit 1 of Aerodynamics II), but reduces lift slope by about cosΛ and tends to produce tip-stall because of spanwise flow; fences, vortex generators and notches help.
- **Winglets/raked tips** diffuse the tip vortex and raise effective span: induced drag is reduced by 3–6% in cruise on airliners (a few % fuel).
- **Effective AR**: end plates raise e; a winglet of height h is roughly equivalent to extra span 0.5–1×h.
- **Wake turbulence**: tip vortices of heavy aircraft persist for minutes; ATC separation standards (e.g. heavier aircraft need longer spacing behind) account for them.

steps.title: Solved example: induced drag saved
steps.body: Wing S = 120 m² and b = 36 m (AR = 10.8), cruise CL = 0.5, e = 0.8. Winglets raise e to 0.85. CDi before = 0.25/(π×0.8×10.8) = 0.00921; after = 0.25/(π×0.85×10.8) = 0.00867. Reduction = 5.9% of induced drag.

steps.title: Solved example: lift slope with sweep
steps.body: Straight wing a = 5.0 /rad; sweep of 30° reduces the slope roughly by cos30° = 0.866 (first-order estimate) → ≈ 4.3 /rad.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming that winglets are a free lunch: they add weight, wetted area and bending moment at the root.
- Confusing aerodynamic washout with structural aeroelastic washout.

steps.title: Polar and L/D

**CD = CD0 + CL²/(π e AR)**. L/D = CL/CD. Maximum L/D occurs when CD0 = CDi: **CL* = √(π e AR CD0)**, **(L/D)max = ½√(π e AR/CD0)**.

lessons.title: Prandtl's boundary-layer concept and thickness definitions

story.title: Why a thin layer rules drag

scenes.text: Air has tiny viscosity, yet a no-slip wall forces velocity to zero at the surface.
In 1904 Prandtl showed that viscous effects live in a thin layer next to the wall; outside it the flow is ideal.

steps.title: Concept
steps.body:
At high Re the viscous region is a thin **boundary layer** of thickness δ ≪ L. Inside, u rises from 0 (no-slip) to ≈ U_e (edge velocity). Prandtl's order-of-magnitude analysis of the Navier–Stokes equations gives, for steady 2-D incompressible flow:

**u ∂u/∂x + v ∂u/∂y = −(1/ρ) dp/dx + ν ∂²u/∂y²**, **∂p/∂y ≈ 0** (pressure imposed by the outer flow, dp/dx = −ρU_e dU_e/dx), plus continuity.

**Definitions**: δ is where u = 0.99 U_e. **Displacement thickness δ\* = ∫₀^∞ (1 − u/U_e) dy** (streamlines pushed outward). **Momentum thickness θ = ∫₀^∞ (u/U_e)(1 − u/U_e) dy**; shape factor H = δ\*/θ (≈ 2.59 laminar flat plate, ≈ 1.3–1.4 turbulent). Wall shear τ_w = μ(∂u/∂y)_w; **Cf = τ_w/(½ρU_e²)**. Momentum-integral (von Kármán): dθ/dx = Cf/2 for zero pressure gradient.

steps.title: Solved example: thicknesses for a linear profile
steps.body:
Take u/U = y/δ for y ≤ δ. δ\* = ∫(1 − y/δ)dy = δ/2. θ = ∫(y/δ)(1 − y/δ)dy = δ/2 − δ/3 = δ/6. H = 3.
With δ = 3 mm: δ\* = 1.5 mm, θ = 0.5 mm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating δ as sharp: it is defined by a 99% convention.
- Forgetting that δ\* is a streamline displacement, not a thickness of any fluid.
- Applying boundary-layer equations near separation or at the leading edge, where they break down.

steps.title: Blasius solution
steps.body:
With similarity variable η = y√(U/(νx)), f‴ + ½ f f″ = 0 (f(0) = f′(0) = 0, f′(∞) = 1), solved numerically, give (Re_x = Ux/ν):

- **δ = 5.0 x/√Re_x**
- **δ\* = 1.721 x/√Re_x**
- **θ = 0.664 x/√Re_x**
- **Cf,x = 0.664/√Re_x**
- Average over length L (one side): **C_D = 1.328/√Re_L**

Drag D = C_D q L per unit width (per side). Valid for Re_L ≲ 5×10⁵ (laminar). Laminar skin friction ∝ U^{1.5}: reducing it is why laminar-flow wings are attractive.

scenes.text: Wind-tunnel model builders glue a thin trip strip near the leading edge to force turbulence and mimic full-scale Re.
You compare laminar, turbulent and mixed estimates for a 2 m plate.

steps.title: Turbulent correlations
steps.body:
Using the 1/7 power law u/U = (y/δ)^{1/7} and the momentum integral (5×10⁵ < Re_x < 10⁷):

- **δ = 0.37 x/Re_x^{0.2}**
- **Cf,x = 0.0592/Re_x^{0.2}**
- **C_D = 0.074/Re_L^{0.2}** (fully turbulent from the leading edge)
- **Mixed laminar–turbulent**, transition at Re_cr = 5×10⁵: **C_D = 0.074/Re_L^{0.2} − 1742/Re_L**
- Schlichting: C_D = 0.455/(log₁₀Re_L)^{2.58} (up to Re ~10⁹).

Turbulent boundary layers are thicker, grow faster (δ ∝ x^0.8), have a fuller profile, more wall shear (Cf larger) but resist separation better.

steps.body:

- Forgetting the 1742/Re correction.
- Assuming turbulence is always bad: it prevents separation (golf balls, vortex generators).

lessons.title: Pressure gradients, transition and separation

story.title: The dimples on a golf ball

scenes.text: A smooth ball would drive 40% shorter: dimples trip the boundary layer so that it clings longer.
Cricketers exploit the same physics: seam and swing.

steps.title: Pressure gradient
steps.body:
- **Favourable (dp/dx < 0)**: flow accelerates, profile fills, stable, delays transition.
- **Adverse (dp/dx > 0)**: flow decelerates; low-momentum fluid near the wall may reverse.
- **Separation** occurs where **(∂u/∂y)_w = 0**, then backflow forms; the separated shear layer produces a wide wake with large **pressure (form) drag** and loss of lift (stall).
- Laminar layers separate under a mild adverse gradient; turbulent layers have more near-wall momentum and survive stronger gradients.
- **Transition** (laminar → turbulent) depends on Re, pressure gradient, roughness, free-stream turbulence, wall temperature; Tollmien–Schlichting waves → spots → turbulence.
- **Laminar separation bubble**: separates, transitions, reattaches (common on airfoils at low Re).
- **Control**: vortex generators, suction, blowing, slots, riblets.

steps.title: Solved example: cylinder drag crisis
steps.body: For a cylinder CD ≈ 1.2 for subcritical flow (laminar separation at ≈ 80° from front) and ≈ 0.3–0.4 after the drag crisis at Re ≈ 3×10⁵ (turbulent boundary layer separates at ≈ 120°, narrower wake). A golf ball of d = 42.7 mm at 60 m/s: Re = 60×0.0427/1.46×10⁻⁵ = 1.75×10⁵, near the crisis: dimples lower the critical Re.

steps.title: Solved example: location of transition
steps.body: Ue = 30 m/s, Re_cr = 5×10⁵ at ν = 1.46×10⁻⁵: x_tr = 5×10⁵×1.46×10⁻⁵/30 = 0.243 m. A rough surface or turbulence moves it forward.

lessons.title: Drag build-up and the drag polar

scenes.text: A small-aircraft designer wants to know which parts of the airplane are costing the most drag.
She builds a component drag table: wing, fuselage, tail, gear, interference.

steps.title: Types of drag
steps.body:
- **Skin-friction drag** (shear on wetted surface).
- **Form/pressure drag** (separation, wake).
- **Interference drag** (junctions, e.g. wing–fuselage).
- **Induced drag** (lift-dependent).
- **Wave drag** (supersonic/transonic, Aerodynamics II).
- **Parasite drag = everything not induced**: CD0.

**Drag polar**: CD = CD0 + K CL², K = 1/(π e AR). **Equivalent parasite (flat-plate) area f = CD0·S** (m²) is a convenient size for comparing aircraft; drag at speed V: D_0 = ½ρV² f. Cleaner designs have f smaller for the same S. Retractable gear and flush rivets reduce f; typical CD0: sailplane 0.012, light aircraft 0.025, airliner 0.020 (clean), fighter 0.015–0.02 (clean).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Light aircraft CD0 = 0.025, S = 16 m², V = 60 m/s sea level: f = 0.4 m². q = 2205 Pa. Parasite drag D_0 = 2205×0.4 = **882 N**.
If fixed landing gear adds f = 0.06 m², extra drag = 132 N, power at 60 m/s = 132×60 = 7.9 kW.

steps.title: Solved example: how drag scales
steps.body: Parasite drag ∝ V². Going from 60 to 90 m/s: ×2.25 → 1,985 N. Induced drag ∝ 1/V² at fixed weight: it falls ×0.44. Minimum drag speed is where they are equal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding CD0 of components referred to different areas without converting to S_ref.
- Treating CD0 as constant at all CL (it grows with CL near stall).
- Confusing wetted area with reference area.

steps.title: Devices
steps.body:
- **Trailing-edge flaps**: plain, split, slotted, double-slotted, **Fowler** (move aft and down, increasing both camber and area); they raise cl,max and shift α_L0 more negative.
- **Leading-edge devices**: slat (opens a slot, re-energises upper-surface flow, raises stall α by 5–10°), Krueger flap, droop nose.
- **Boundary-layer control**: blowing/suction, blown flaps (STOL aircraft).
- Penalties: weight, complexity, high drag (also used as speed brakes/steep approach), nose-down pitching moment and trim change.

Typical 2-D increments in cl,max: about 0.9 (plain), 1.5 (slotted), 1.3–1.6 (Fowler); with slats an airliner reaches CL,max of 3.0 or more at landing.

steps.title: Solved example: landing roll sensitivity
steps.body: Landing distance ∝ V². Reducing Vs by 20% cuts the ground roll to (0.797)² = 63.5% of the clean value: a 36% reduction.

- Saying 'flaps increase stall speed'. They lower it (but they increase drag, so approach attitude/power changes).
- Ignoring the extra nose-down moment: the tail must trim it.
- Using clean CL,max for the flap-extended case.

steps.title: Facilities and methods
steps.body:
- **Open-circuit (Eiffel)** tunnels: cheap, noisy, laboratory-air dependent. **Closed-circuit (Göttingen)**: quieter, better flow quality, energy efficient.
- Components: settling chamber with honeycomb and screens (reduce turbulence), contraction (ratio 6–9), test section, diffuser (angle < 7° total), fan/drive.
- Measurements: **pressure** (Pitot-static, manometer, scanner), **forces** (internal/external balance), **flow visualisation** (tufts, smoke, oil film), **velocity** (hot-wire, LDV, PIV).
- Dynamic pressure from a water manometer: **q = ρ_w g Δh** and V = √(2q/ρ).
- **Corrections**: solid blockage and wake blockage (model area/test section area < 10%), streamline curvature, tunnel walls, support interference (tare). Reynolds number mismatch is the main scale issue.
- **Data reduction**: CL = L/(qS), CD = D/(qS), CM; subtract tares.

steps.title: Bluff-body drag
steps.body:
Drag **D = CD · ½ρV² · A_ref** where A_ref is frontal projected area (for a cylinder d×L). Typical CD (Re-dependent): long cylinder 1.2 (subcritical), sphere 0.47, flat plate normal to flow 1.1–2.0, disc 1.17, cube 1.05, streamlined strut 0.04–0.06, cars 0.25–0.35, cyclist 0.7–0.9 (with area), parachute 1.3–1.5.

Streamlining reduces CD by moving separation aft. **Vortex shedding** at Strouhal number **St = f d/V ≈ 0.2** can excite structures (Tacoma Narrows-type aeroelastic effects, helical strakes on chimneys).

lessons.title: Formula and key-point sheet

scenes.text: A student has one hour to revise the whole of Aerodynamics I.

steps.title: Atmosphere, airspeed, similarity
steps.body:
- ISA: T = 288.15 − 0.0065h; p/p0 = (T/T0)^5.2559; ρ/ρ0 = (T/T0)^4.2559 (0–11 km); isothermal above, 216.65 K.
- q = ½ρV² (Pa); Bernoulli p + q = p0; continuity A1V1 = A2V2.
- Re = ρVL/μ; M = V/a; a = √(γRT); Cp = 1 − (V/V∞)².
- TAS = EAS/√σ; σ = ρ/ρ0.
- Pitot: V = √(2Δp/ρ).

steps.title: Potential flow and airfoils
steps.body:
- Source V_r = Λ/(2πr); vortex V_θ = Γ/(2πr); doublet ∝ 1/r².
- Cylinder: Cp = 1 − 4sin²θ; lifting: L′ = ρV∞Γ.
- Thin airfoil: cl = 2π(α − α_L0); cm,c/4 constant; ac at c/4; cm,le = cm,c/4 − cl/4; xcp = −cm,le/cl.
- NACA MPXX: camber %, position tenths, thickness %.

steps.title: Finite wings and viscous flow
steps.body:
- AR = b²/S; λ = c_t/c_r; MAC = (2/3)c_r(1+λ+λ²)/(1+λ).
- Elliptic: α_i = CL/(πAR); CDi = CL²/(πeAR); Γ0 = 2VSCL/(πb); a = a0/(1 + a0/(πAR)).
- Blasius: δ = 5x/√Re; Cf = 0.664/√Re; CD = 1.328/√Re_L.
- Turbulent: δ = 0.37x/Re^0.2; CD = 0.074/Re_L^0.2 (− 1742/Re_L mixed).
- (L/D)max = ½√(πeAR/CD0) at CL = √(πeARCD0); Pr = DV.

steps.title: Top mistakes to avoid
steps.body:
- Degrees vs radians in 2π(α − α_L0).
- Forgetting √σ in TAS.
- Using a0 for a wing; using AR rather than π AR.
- Using laminar formulas beyond Re ≈ 5×10⁵.

steps.title: Aim, apparatus, procedure
steps.body:
**Aim**: traverse a total-pressure probe through the boundary layer on a flat plate, compute δ, δ\*, θ and H, and compare laminar/turbulent profiles.
**Procedure**: place the plate with a sharp leading edge, mount a flattened Pitot probe on a micrometer traverse, measure p0(y) at x = 0.3 m for U = 15 m/s; compute u(y) = √(2(p0 − p)/ρ); integrate.
**Typical results** (turbulent): δ = 7 mm, δ\* = 0.9 mm, θ = 0.7 mm, H = 1.3. Laminar: H ≈ 2.6.

steps.title: Worked data reduction
steps.body: At the 5 mm position p0 − p = 100 Pa: u = √(200/1.225) = 12.8 m/s; with U = 15: u/U = 0.85. For a 1/7-power turbulent profile, y/δ = 0.85^7 = 0.32; with δ = 7 mm this is 2.2 mm — so the measured 5 mm point shows the BL is *fuller* or thicker than the idealised case; compare in the report.

steps.body: Probe displacement effect near the wall, finite probe size, turbulence intensity, plate not aligned.

items.q: Why is the velocity zero at the wall?

items.q: Why is a turbulent boundary layer better at resisting separation?
items.a: Turbulent mixing brings high-momentum fluid near the wall, giving a fuller profile and larger near-wall shear.

items.q: What is H and what does it tell you?

items.q: Why do we use trip strips on models?
items.a: To fix transition and match full-scale boundary-layer states at lower Re.

items.a: The smoke streakline coincides with streamlines in steady flow.

items.q: What is d'Alembert's paradox and how is it resolved?
items.a: Ideal flow predicts zero drag; viscosity and separation create a wake and pressure drag.

lessons.title: Speed of sound, Mach number and flow regimes

story.title: Breaking the sound barrier at 10 km

scenes.text: A jet airliner at 10 km flies at 250 m/s. Its pilots quote Mach number, not speed.
The speed of sound depends only on temperature, so the same Mach number means different speeds at different altitudes.

steps.title: Derivation of the speed of sound
steps.body:
A small pressure disturbance travels as a wave. Apply conservation of mass and momentum across a stationary weak wave (control volume): a = √(dp/dρ) at constant entropy. For a calorically perfect gas, isentropic p/ρ^γ = const gives dp/dρ = γp/ρ = γRT, so

**a = √(γ R T)** (air: γ = 1.4, R = 287.05 J/kg·K; a = 20.05√T m/s).

**Mach number M = V/a.** Regimes: incompressible M < 0.3; subsonic 0.3 < M < 0.8; transonic 0.8–1.2 (mixed subsonic/supersonic pockets); supersonic 1.2–5; hypersonic M > 5 (chemically reacting, aerothermal heating).

**Mach angle** of a weak wave from a supersonic source: μ = sin⁻¹(1/M). Zone of silence ahead of the source for M > 1.

steps.title: Solved example: Mach angle
steps.body: A fighter at M = 2 produces a Mach wave with μ = sin⁻¹(0.5) = **30°**. If it flies at 5 km altitude directly overhead, the sound arrives after it has moved ahead by h/tanμ = 5000/0.5774 = 8.66 km.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C in a = √(γRT).
- Thinking Mach number is fixed to speed: M depends on local a.
- Saying 'sound barrier' = Mach 1 exactly; transonic effects begin at M_cr (~0.7–0.85).

story.title: How hot does the nose get?

scenes.text: The nose of a Mach 2 fighter at 11 km heats to about 117 °C even in the cold stratosphere.
Stagnation temperature tells designers how hot the skin will get.

steps.title: Energy equation and stagnation conditions
steps.body:
Steady adiabatic flow: h + V²/2 = h0 (constant), so with cp = γR/(γ−1): **T0/T = 1 + ((γ−1)/2) M²**. For isentropic flow:

- **p0/p = (1 + 0.2M²)^3.5**
- **ρ0/ρ = (1 + 0.2M²)^2.5**
- T0 stays constant in any adiabatic flow (including across shocks); p0 stays constant only in isentropic flow.

**Critical (sonic) values** (M = 1): T*/T0 = 0.8333, p*/p0 = 0.5283, ρ*/ρ0 = 0.6339. Table values: M = 0.5 → T0/T = 1.05, p0/p = 1.186; M = 0.8 → 1.128, 1.524; M = 2 → 1.8, 7.824; M = 3 → 2.8, 36.73.

steps.title: Solved example: aircraft at M = 0.8, 10 km
steps.body: T = 223.15 K, p = 26,436 Pa. T0 = 223.15×1.128 = **251.7 K**. p0 = 26,436×1.5243 = **40,297 Pa**. A pitot probe on the nose senses p0 (subsonic, no shock).

lessons.title: Area–velocity relation, area–Mach number and choking

scenes.text: Subsonic flow speeds up in a narrowing duct, but supersonic flow speeds up only in a widening one.
The throat is where the flow reaches M = 1 — it is choked.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body:
From continuity and Euler: **dA/A = (M² − 1) dV/V**.
- M < 1: A decreases as V increases (converging nozzle accelerates, diverging diffuser decelerates).
- M > 1: A must increase as V increases (diverging section accelerates).
- M = 1 only at a minimum area (throat), A*.

**Area–Mach relation** (isentropic): **A/A\* = (1/M)[(2/(γ+1))(1 + ((γ−1)/2)M²)]^{(γ+1)/(2(γ−1))}** = (1/M)[(1 + 0.2M²)/1.2]³. For a given A/A* > 1 there are two solutions: subsonic and supersonic.

Table (γ = 1.4): M = 0.5 → 1.340; M = 2 → 1.688; M = 2.5 → 2.637; M = 3 → 4.235.

**Choked mass flow**: ṁ = 0.0404 p0 A*/√T0 (SI, air) = p0 A* √(γ/(R T0)) (2/(γ+1))^{(γ+1)/(2(γ−1))}.

steps.title: Solved example: exit area
steps.body: Throat A* = 0.010 m², exit Mach 2: A_e = 1.6875×0.010 = **0.016875 m²** (exit diameter 14.7 cm if circular).

steps.title: Solved example: choked mass flow
steps.body: p0 = 500 kPa, T0 = 300 K, A* = 0.010 m²: ṁ = 0.0404×500,000×0.010/√300 = 202.1/17.32 = **11.67 kg/s**. Reducing the back pressure does not increase ṁ once choked; raising p0 does (ṁ ∝ p0).

steps.body:

- Assuming ṁ increases as you lower back pressure after choking.
- Using A (actual) instead of A* in the mass flow formula.

lessons.title: Lab: Operating regimes of a convergent–divergent nozzle

scenes.text: In a laboratory blow-down rig, you lower the back pressure step by step and watch the wall-pressure traces.
Each curve corresponds to a different flow regime.

steps.title: Regimes for A_e/A* = 1.6875
steps.body:
With reservoir p0 fixed and p_b the back pressure:
1. **p_b/p0 > 0.909** (first critical): subsonic everywhere, throat not choked, venturi behaviour.
2. **0.909 > p_b/p0 > 0.575**: choked throat, a normal shock stands inside the diverging section; subsonic exit.
3. **p_b/p0 = 0.575 (second critical)**: the normal shock sits at the exit plane (0.1278×4.5).
4. **0.575 > p_b/p0 > 0.1278**: **over-expanded**: oblique shocks outside the exit.
5. **p_b/p0 = 0.1278 (third/design)**: shock-free, M_e = 2.
6. **p_b/p0 < 0.1278**: **under-expanded**: Prandtl–Meyer expansion fans outside.

The first critical value comes from the subsonic root of A/A* = 1.6875 (M ≈ 0.372, p/p0 = 0.909).

steps.title: Solved example: reservoir 700 kPa
steps.body:
Design back pressure = 0.1278×700 = **89.5 kPa**; shock-at-exit pressure = 0.575×700 = **402.6 kPa**; first critical = 0.909×700 = **636 kPa**.
If ambient is 101 kPa, which is above the design value of 89.5 kPa, the nozzle is over-expanded (oblique shocks at the lip). If ambient were 60 kPa it would be under-expanded.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing 'over-expanded' (p_e < p_b) with 'under-expanded' (p_e > p_b).
- Thinking a shock in the nozzle makes the throat unchoked: the throat remains choked.

lessons.title: Lab: Normal shock waves

scenes.text: A sonic boom is a pressure jump that spreads from an aircraft over a few milliseconds.
A normal shock is a thin (≈ 10⁻⁷ m) region where supersonic flow suddenly becomes subsonic.

steps.title: Conservation across the shock
steps.body:
For a stationary normal shock (1 = upstream, 2 = downstream):
- Mass: ρ1u1 = ρ2u2
- Momentum: p1 + ρ1u1² = p2 + ρ2u2²
- Energy: h1 + u1²/2 = h2 + u2²/2 (T0 constant)

Results (γ = 1.4):
- **M2² = (1 + 0.2M1²)/(1.4M1² − 0.2)**
- **p2/p1 = 1 + (2γ/(γ+1))(M1² − 1) = 1 + 1.1667(M1² − 1)**
- **ρ2/ρ1 = (γ+1)M1²/((γ−1)M1² + 2) = 2.4M1²/(0.4M1² + 2)** (max 6 as M1 → ∞)
- **T2/T1 = (p2/p1)(ρ1/ρ2)**
- Total pressure loss p02/p01 < 1 (entropy rises): Δs = −R ln(p02/p01).

A shock can exist only if M1 > 1 (an expansion shock violates the second law).

steps.title: Solved example: M1 = 3 and entropy rise
Common mistakes
steps.body:

- Using p02/p01 with static ratios.
- Forgetting that T0 is conserved across the shock but p0 is not.

lessons.title: Lab: Pitot probes in supersonic flow (Rayleigh pitot formula)

story.title: What does a pitot tube read at Mach 2?

scenes.text: A blunt pitot probe in a supersonic stream creates a detached bow shock; the probe reads total pressure behind the normal shock part.
The airspeed system uses the ratio of that pressure to static pressure to compute M.

steps.title: Rayleigh pitot formula
steps.body:
For M1 > 1 the probe reads p02 (behind a normal shock, then isentropic deceleration):

**p02/p1 = [ (γ+1)²M1² / (4γM1² − 2(γ−1)) ]^{γ/(γ−1)} × [ (1 − γ + 2γM1²)/(γ+1) ]**
(= (p02/p01)·(p01/p1)).

For γ = 1.4: M1 = 1.5 → 3.413; M1 = 2 → **5.640**; M1 = 3 → 12.06. The static pressure p1 is measured separately (static port); M is obtained by iteration/table. For M < 1, p0/p = (1 + 0.2M²)^3.5 applies instead.

steps.title: Solved example: inverse problem
steps.body: p02/p1 measured = 12.06 → M1 = 3. A ratio of 3.413 → M1 = 1.5. Interpolating: ratio 4.5 → M1 ≈ 1.76.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the isentropic formula above M = 1 (it overestimates p0 by far).
- Believing the pitot reads the free-stream total pressure p01 in supersonic flow.

lessons.title: Lab: Fanno flow – adiabatic flow in a constant-area duct with friction

scenes.text: A compressed-air line 50 mm in diameter feeds a tool at M = 0.5 at its inlet.
Friction lowers the pressure; if the pipe is too long, the flow chokes at the exit and the mass flow drops.

steps.title: Fanno line
steps.body:
Constant area, adiabatic, with wall friction: T0 const; entropy increases; both subsonic and supersonic flow approach **M = 1** (choking) at the length L*.

**4 f_F L*/D = (1 − M²)/(γM²) + ((γ+1)/(2γ)) ln[ (γ+1)M² / (2 + (γ−1)M²) ]** (f_F = Fanning friction factor; with Darcy f_D the left side is f_D L*/D).

Properties relative to the sonic state: T/T* = 1.2/(1 + 0.2M²); p/p* = (1/M)√(1.2/(1 + 0.2M²)); p0/p0* = (1/M)[(1 + 0.2M²)/1.2]³.
Table: M = 0.5 → 4fL*/D = 1.0691, T/T* = 1.1429, p/p* = 2.138; M = 2 → 0.3050.
Subsonic flow: friction raises M (toward 1), lowers p and T. Supersonic: friction lowers M, raises p and T.

steps.title: Solved example: exit Mach of a 2 m pipe
steps.body: For L = 2 m: 4f_F L/D = 4×0.005×2/0.05 = 0.80. The remaining Fanno parameter at the exit is 1.0691 − 0.80 = 0.269, which (solving the Fanno equation) corresponds to an exit Mach number of about M2 = 0.67. Friction has raised M from 0.5 to 0.67 while the static pressure has fallen.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing Fanning and Darcy friction factors (factor 4).
- Assuming friction can push subsonic flow past M = 1.
- Neglecting that choking reduces mass flow when the duct is longer than L*.

lessons.title: Lab: Rayleigh flow – heat addition in a constant-area duct

scenes.text: Burning fuel adds heat in a nearly constant-area combustor.
There is a maximum heat that can be added before the flow chokes — thermal choking.

steps.title: Rayleigh line
steps.body:
Constant area, frictionless, with heat addition q (J/kg): q = cp(T02 − T01). Relations (γ = 1.4):

- **T0/T0\* = (γ+1)M²[2 + (γ−1)M²]/(1 + γM²)² = 2.4M²(2 + 0.4M²)/(1 + 1.4M²)²**
- **p/p\* = (γ+1)/(1 + γM²)**
- **T/T\* = [(γ+1)M/(1 + γM²)]²**

Heating drives M toward 1 (from either side). Subsonic: heating raises M; p falls. Table: M = 0.5 → T0/T0* = 0.6914, p/p* = 1.778; M = 2 → 0.7934. Maximum entropy at M = 1; maximum T at M = 1/√γ = 0.845.

steps.title: Solved example: pressure drop
steps.body: At M1 = 0.5: p1/p* = 1.778. At the choked exit p2 = p*, so p2/p1 = 1/1.778 = **0.5625**: a 44% static pressure loss (an unavoidable 'Rayleigh loss' on top of flow acceleration).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using cp = 1.4 instead of 1005 J/(kg·K).
- Expecting heat addition to always increase M: it decreases M in supersonic flow.
- Confusing static and total temperatures.

lessons.title: Lab: Oblique shock waves

scenes.text: A supersonic wedge forces the flow to turn by θ; the flow responds with an attached straight oblique shock.
The trick: treat the velocity component normal to the shock as a normal shock.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
Let β be the shock angle to the upstream direction and θ the flow deflection. Resolve the velocity: normal component u_n = V sinβ, tangential component constant across the shock. Hence M_n1 = M1 sinβ and the normal-shock relations apply with M1 replaced by M_n1:
- **p2/p1 = 1 + 1.1667(M_n1² − 1)**, ρ2/ρ1, T2/T1 as for normal shocks.
- **M_n2² = (1 + 0.2M_n1²)/(1.4M_n1² − 0.2)** and **M2 = M_n2/sin(β − θ)**.

**θ–β–M relation**: **tanθ = 2cotβ (M1²sin²β − 1)/(M1²(γ + cos2β) + 2)**. For given M1 and θ ≤ θ_max there are two β: weak (usual, M2 supersonic) and strong (M2 subsonic). Mach wave limit: β = μ = sin⁻¹(1/M1) (θ = 0).

steps.title: Solved example: M1 = 3, θ = 20°
steps.body: β = 37.8°; M_n1 = 3 sin37.76° = 1.837, M_n1² = 3.374; p2/p1 = 1 + 1.1667×2.374 = **3.77**; ρ2/ρ1 = 2.418; T2/T1 = 1.559; M_n2 = 0.6085, M2 = 0.6085/sin17.76° = **1.99**. Total pressure ratio ≈ 0.80, compared with 0.33 for a normal shock at M = 3: oblique shocks are far more efficient.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using M1 instead of M_n1 in the normal-shock relations.
- Dividing M_n2 by sinβ instead of sin(β − θ).
- Using the strong solution unintentionally; real wedges with attached flow take the weak solution.

lessons.title: Lab: Using the θ–β–M diagram, detached shocks and wall reflection

story.title: When the wedge is too steep

scenes.text: At Mach 2 a wedge steeper than about 23° cannot keep the shock attached.
A curved, detached bow shock stands ahead of the body.

steps.title: Maximum deflection and detachment
steps.body:
For each M1 there is θ_max (M1 = 2: 22.97°; M1 = 3: 34.1°; M1 → ∞: 45.6°). If θ > θ_max the shock **detaches**: it is a curved bow shock with a normal portion on the axis (stagnation streamline), oblique further out (weak), and a subsonic region near the body. Blunt noses always produce detached shocks.

**Reflection from a wall**: the oblique shock from a wedge at the opposite wall requires the flow to be turned back parallel to the wall; the reflected shock turns the flow by the same θ using M2 as the new upstream Mach number. **Regular reflection** is possible only if the required deflection ≤ θ_max(M2); otherwise Mach reflection.

steps.title: Solved example: detachment check
steps.body: A 25° wedge in M = 2 flow: θ_max = 22.97° < 25° → **detached bow shock**. A 15° wedge is attached with β ≈ 45.3°.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the chart for θ > θ_max.
- Treating wall reflection as a mirror of θ and β, not of the flow deflection.
- Forgetting that pressure ratios multiply through successive shocks, but the total pressure losses compound too.

statements.why: Wall boundary condition requires V parallel to the wall.

statements.s: At θ = 0 the weak oblique shock becomes a normal shock.
statements.why: At θ = 0 the weak solution is a Mach wave; the strong one is a normal shock.

lessons.title: Lab: Prandtl–Meyer expansion fans

scenes.text: Supersonic flow turning away from itself (an expansion corner) does not shock: it fans out through an infinite number of Mach waves.
The Prandtl–Meyer function ν(M) tells you how much the flow has turned from M = 1.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body:
An isentropic expansion through a centred fan of Mach waves between angles μ1 = sin⁻¹(1/M1) and μ2 = sin⁻¹(1/M2). Integrating dθ = √(M² − 1) dV/V gives the **Prandtl–Meyer function** (γ = 1.4):

**ν(M) = √6 tan⁻¹√((M² − 1)/6) − tan⁻¹√(M² − 1)**, ν(1) = 0, ν_max = 130.45° (M → ∞).

For a turn θ: **ν(M2) = ν(M1) + θ** (expansion). Then p0, T0 are constant: use isentropic ratios for p2/p1 and T2/T1.
Table: ν(1.5) = 11.91°; ν(2) = 26.38°; ν(2.5) = 39.12°; ν(3) = 49.76°.

steps.title: Solved example: fan extent
steps.body: μ1 = sin⁻¹(1/2) = 30°; μ2 = sin⁻¹(1/2.386) = 24.8°. The first (leading) Mach wave makes 30° with the upstream wall; the last (trailing) wave makes 24.8° with the downstream wall, which is itself turned 10° away. The fan therefore spans 30° − (24.8° − 10°) = 15.2° between its first and last waves.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding θ in the wrong direction: expansion increases ν, compression decreases it.
- Evaluating the arctangent terms in degrees and multiplying by √6 without care: compute in radians, then convert.
- Expecting a total-pressure loss: Prandtl–Meyer expansion is isentropic.

lessons.title: Lab: Shock–expansion theory for a flat plate

scenes.text: A thin fin at 5° incidence in a Mach 2 stream is modelled as a flat plate.
The top surface sees expansion, the bottom surface an oblique shock.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
1. Upper surface: expansion by α → ν_u = ν1 + α → M_u → p_u/p1 (isentropic).
2. Lower surface: oblique shock of deflection α → p_l/p1 (weak solution).
3. **q1 = (γ/2) p1 M1²** so Cp = (p/p1 − 1)/(0.7M1²).
4. Forces: **cl = (Cp_l − Cp_u) cosα**, **cd = (Cp_l − Cp_u) sinα** (wave drag), **cm** about the leading edge from c/2 pressure centre.

steps.title: Solved example: linear-theory check
steps.body: Ackeret: cl = 4α/√(M²−1) = 4×0.08727/1.732 = **0.2015**; cd = 4α²/√(M²−1) = 4×0.007615/1.732 = **0.0176**. Agreement within 1% for this small α. Lift-to-drag ratio = 1/α = 11.5 — note that it is cotα for a flat plate: all of the drag is wave drag.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using cl = (Cp_l − Cp_u) without cosα (fine for small α only).
- Dropping skin friction: real drag also includes CD,f ≈ 0.003–0.006 (laminar/turbulent).
- Using the strong oblique shock solution.

steps.title: Design idea
steps.body: Replace one strong normal shock by several weaker oblique shocks followed by a weak normal shock at the throat (Oswatitsch optimum: equal normal Mach numbers across each shock minimises loss). Recovery = product of p0 ratios.

steps.title: Solved example: M1 = 2.0, one-ramp intake
steps.body:
Ramp: θ = 10°, M2 = 1.641, p02/p01 ≈ 0.984 (weak shock with M_n1 = 1.267).
Then a normal shock at M2 = 1.641: p02/p01 ≈ 0.879.
Total ≈ 0.984×0.879 = **0.865**, versus **0.721** for a single normal shock: a gain of about 20% in available total pressure.

steps.body: With free-stream p01 = 177 kPa (M = 2 at 11 km): normal-shock recovery gives 127.6 kPa; the ramp intake gives about 153 kPa. Higher compressor-face pressure raises cycle efficiency and thrust.

- Ignoring boundary-layer bleed, which is essential on real intakes.
- Assuming more ramps always help; weight and drag rise.
- Forgetting that the final normal shock must remain stable ('critical' intake operation).

steps.title: The linearised potential equation
steps.body:
For a thin body at small angle in a nearly uniform subsonic stream, the velocity potential satisfies (1 − M∞²) φ_xx + φ_yy = 0. With β = √(1 − M∞²) and the transformation x′ = x, y′ = βy, the equation becomes Laplace's equation. The result is the **Prandtl–Glauert rule**:

**Cp = Cp,0/√(1 − M∞²)**, **cl = cl,0/√(1 − M∞²)**, **cm = cm,0/√(1 − M∞²)**, where the subscript 0 means the incompressible value for the same shape and α.

Valid roughly for M∞ < 0.7 and thin sections at small α; it fails at transonic speeds (singular at M∞ = 1). A better empirical rule is **Kármán–Tsien**; the lift slope grows as 1/β.

steps.title: Solved example: lift coefficient
steps.body: cl,0 = 0.60 at M∞ ≈ 0. At M∞ = 0.8: cl = 0.60/0.6 = **1.00**. So for a given α, the lift is 67% higher than the incompressible value. For constant lift (cruise) the airplane needs a lower α at high M.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the rule near M = 1 (it blows up).
- Applying it to thick sections or high α.
- Forgetting that it applies to the *same shape*, not the same lift.

lessons.title: Lab: Critical Mach number

story.title: When the first pocket of supersonic air appears

scenes.text: As free-stream Mach rises, the suction peak accelerates the local flow faster than the free stream.
The critical Mach number M_cr is when local M first reaches 1 anywhere on the aircraft.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
Isentropic relation between Cp and local Mach M: **Cp = (2/(γM∞²)) { [ (1 + 0.2M∞²)/(1 + 0.2M²) ]^3.5 − 1 }**. At the sonic point M = 1 this gives the **critical pressure coefficient**:

**Cp,cr = (2/(γ M_cr²)) { [ (1 + 0.2 M_cr²)/1.2 ]^3.5 − 1 }**.

The curve Cp,cr(M∞) falls with M∞. The Prandtl–Glauert curve Cp,min(M∞) = Cp,0/√(1 − M∞²) also falls (becomes more negative). **M_cr is their intersection** (found by iteration or graph). Thinner sections and lower lift (smaller |Cp,0|) give higher M_cr.

Values: Cp,cr(0.6) = −1.29; Cp,cr(0.7) = −0.779; Cp,cr(0.8) = −0.435; Cp,cr(0.9) = −0.188.

steps.title: Solved example: critical speed
steps.body: At 10 km (a = 299.5 m/s): V_cr = 0.716×299.5 = **214 m/s** (772 km/h). A thinner wing with Cp,0 = −0.3 would have M_cr ≈ 0.79, i.e. about 237 m/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking Cp,cr from a table at the wrong M.
- Using Cp,0 of the whole aircraft: the wing, fuselage and canopy each have their own M_cr; the lowest governs.
- Confusing M_cr (first sonic point) with the drag-divergence Mach number (drag rise begins), which is higher.

steps.title: Physics
steps.body:
- **Supersonic pocket** ends in a nearly normal shock on the upper surface. As M∞ rises the shock moves aft and strengthens.
- **Drag divergence Mach number M_dd**: where dCD/dM = 0.1. The drag coefficient may double in a Mach increment of 0.05–0.1.
- **Shock-induced separation** and **buffet** (self-sustained shock oscillation) limit the high-speed envelope; **Mach tuck** (nose-down trim change as the centre of pressure moves aft) appears on older swept transports.
- At M ≈ 1.0–1.2 the bow shock forms; above ~1.2 the flow is mostly supersonic and the drag coefficient falls slowly.

**Korn equation** (empirical, for supercritical-type design): **M_dd = κ_A/cosΛ − (t/c)/cos²Λ − CL/(10 cos³Λ)**, κ_A ≈ 0.87 (conventional sections), ≈ 0.95 (supercritical).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Korn's equation in degrees/radians inconsistently (cosΛ is dimensionless).
- Treating M_dd as a hard limit: airliners cruise 0.02–0.05 below.
- Forgetting that increasing CL lowers M_dd.

lessons.title: Sweep, supercritical airfoils and the area rule

scenes.text: In the 1950s some early supersonic interceptors could not pass Mach 1 until their fuselages were re-shaped.
Richard Whitcomb's area rule fixed it: keep the cross-section area distribution smooth.

steps.title: Three tools against wave drag
steps.body:
1. **Sweep** (Busemann, 1935; used widely after WWII): only the velocity component normal to the leading edge matters, **M_n = M∞ cosΛ**. A 35° sweep at M∞ = 0.85 gives M_n = 0.696. Costs: lower lift slope (≈ cosΛ), tip stall, aeroelastic issues, heavier structure.
2. **Supercritical airfoil** (Whitcomb, 1960s–70s): flat upper surface, large leading-edge radius, aft camber with a cusped lower surface; it creates a long, weak supersonic region ending in a much weaker shock, raising M_dd by ≈ 0.07–0.1 or allowing thicker sections (lighter structure).
3. **Area rule** (Whitcomb, 1952): the transonic wave drag of a wing–body combination is close to that of a body of revolution with the same cross-sectional area distribution A(x); reduce A(x) of the fuselage where the wing adds area ('Coke-bottle' fuselage). Supersonic area rule: apply the rule along Mach planes.

steps.title: Solved example: lift-slope penalty
steps.body: Straight-wing slope a = 5.0 /rad. At Λ = 35° the approximate slope is a cosΛ = 4.10 /rad: a 18% loss, offset by landing-flap and slat design.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using M∞ rather than M_n in the airfoil's critical Mach check.
- Believing the area rule removes wave drag: it reduces the *zero-lift wave drag* by smoothing A(x).
- Treating supercritical airfoils as free: they have higher nose-down moments and aft loading.

story.title: Why supersonic wings are thin and sharp

scenes.text: A supersonic fighter's wing has a knife-edge leading edge and a thickness ratio of only a few percent.
Linear theory shows exactly why.

steps.title: Ackeret theory
steps.body:
Small disturbances in supersonic flow obey (M∞² − 1)φ_xx − φ_yy = 0, a wave equation whose solutions are constant along Mach lines. The surface pressure coefficient depends only on the local surface slope:

**Cp = ± 2θ/√(M∞² − 1)** (positive for compression, i.e. a surface turned into the flow).

For a thin airfoil at angle α: **cl = 4α/√(M∞² − 1)**, **cd,w = (4/√(M∞² − 1)) [ α² + (dz_c/dx)²_avg + (dz_t/dx)²_avg ]**, and the aerodynamic centre moves to c/2.

For a **double-wedge** (diamond) section with thickness ratio τ = t/c at α = 0, each surface has slope ±τ (half-angle ε = τ, small), so **cd,w = 4τ²/√(M∞² − 1)**. Wave drag ∝ τ², hence thin sections; it does not vanish with AR (unlike induced drag) — it is a property of volume and lift.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Ackeret formulas at M near 1 or in hypersonic flow where slopes are large.
- Forgetting the thickness term in drag.
- Forgetting that wave drag exists even at zero lift for thick supersonic sections.

lessons.title: Supersonic wing planforms, Mach cone and delta wings

scenes.text: Concorde's slender delta wing flew at Mach 2 with leading edges that stayed 'subsonic' relative to the flow.
Whether a leading edge is subsonic or supersonic decides the pressure distribution and the drag.

steps.title: Mach cone and edge types
steps.body:
A disturbance at a point influences only the downstream **Mach cone** (half-angle μ = sin⁻¹(1/M∞)). Tip and root effects are confined inside the cones from the tips/edges.

For a swept leading edge with sweep Λ_LE: the normal Mach number M_n = M∞ cosΛ_LE. If **M_n < 1** the edge is **subsonic** (edge lies inside the Mach cone from the apex): leading-edge suction, rounded edges, lower wave drag. If **M_n > 1** it is **supersonic**: shock-like behaviour and sharp edges as for 2-D theory.

Rectangular wing in supersonic flow: 2-D theory applies outside the tip Mach cones; inside, the load falls toward zero. Delta wings: lift from spanwise vortices (leading-edge vortices at high α) gives **non-linear vortex lift** at low speed and for slender wings (CL ∝ α + α²-term).

steps.title: Solved example: edge classification
steps.body: M∞ = 2: μ = 30°. Leading-edge sweep 60°: M_n = 2cos60° = 1.0 → sonic; sweep 65°: M_n = 0.845 → **subsonic**; sweep 45°: M_n = 1.414 → **supersonic**. A delta wing with 65° sweep at M = 2 therefore has subsonic leading edges.

steps.title: Solved example: aspect ratio and the βAR parameter
steps.body: Define β = √(M² − 1). For M = 2, β = 1.732. For a rectangular wing with AR = 3: βAR = 5.2. If βAR ≥ ~4 the average lift slope approaches the 2-D value 4/β = 2.31 /rad; for small βAR (slender wings) the slope approaches the slender-wing limit (π/2)AR = 4.7 /rad, so wing slenderness matters.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying 2-D Ackeret to the whole of a low-AR wing.
- Forgetting the Mach cone effect at tips.
- Using M cosΛ with Λ measured from the wrong axis (use sweep from the spanwise normal).

lessons.title: Lab: Wave drag of bodies and the Sears–Haack body

scenes.text: A designer must put a given volume inside a fuselage of given length and wants minimum supersonic wave drag.
Sears and Haack solved this in the 1940s.

steps.title: Slender-body wave drag
steps.body:
For a slender body, the wave drag depends on the second derivative of the cross-section area distribution S(x) (area rule): the **Sears–Haack body** (pointed at both ends, given length l and volume V) has minimum wave drag:

**D_w/q = 128 V²/(π l⁴) = (9π/2)(S_max/l)²**, with S_max = 16V/(3πl) is the maximum cross-section area.

Wave drag coefficient on S_max: C_D = D_w/(q S_max) = (9π/2)(S_max/l²). Slender (large l²/S_max) bodies reduce drag. The area rule also says: the total area distribution (fuselage + wings + tails + engine nacelles, cut by Mach planes) should be smooth.

steps.title: Solved example: slenderness effect
steps.body: Increasing the length from 20 m to 25 m at the same S_max: D_w/q scales as 1/l² → (20/25)² = 0.64: 36% less wave drag (but heavier).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using S_max where V is intended in the V²/l⁴ form.
- Forgetting that the Sears–Haack result is a *lower bound* for given V and l.
- Applying slender-body formulas to fat bodies.

lessons.title: Lab: Hypersonic flow – Newtonian theory and stagnation heating

scenes.text: A capsule re-entering at several km/s compresses the air so violently that its shock layer glows.
Designers need pressure and temperature estimates for the heat shield.

steps.title: Hypersonic features (M > 5)
steps.body:
- **Thin shock layer**: the shock lies very close to the body.
- **Entropy layer** and **viscous interaction**.
- **High-temperature (real-gas) effects**: vibrational excitation, dissociation of O₂ (≥ ~2,500 K) and N₂ (≥ ~4,000 K), ionisation — the γ = 1.4 perfect-gas model fails.
- **Mach-number independence**: pressure and force coefficients become nearly independent of M∞.

**Newtonian theory**: particles hit the surface and lose their normal momentum: **Cp = 2 sin²θ_s** (θ_s = angle between the surface and the free-stream direction), a good estimate on the windward side; leeward Cp ≈ 0. **Cp,max** at the stagnation point is the Rayleigh pitot value: ≈ 1.83 at M = 10 (→ 1.84 as M → ∞); *modified Newtonian*: Cp = Cp,max sin²θ_s.

**Perfect-gas stagnation temperature**: T0 = T∞(1 + 0.2M∞²). Real flight temperature is lower because dissociation absorbs energy.

steps.title: Solved example: wedge
steps.body: A 10° half-angle wedge in hypersonic flow: Newtonian Cp = 2 sin²10° = **0.0603**. The exact oblique-shock value at M = 10 is ≈ 0.086: Newtonian theory under-predicts by about 30% for such a shallow wedge and is better for blunt, steeply inclined surfaces.

steps.title: Solved example: stagnation temperature at M = 10, 30 km
steps.body: T∞ = 226.5 K: T0 = 226.5×(1 + 0.2×100) = **4,756 K** (perfect gas). The actual temperature of the air at the stagnation point is far lower because dissociation absorbs energy: the perfect-gas value is an upper bound. Flight speed V = 10×301.7 = 3,017 m/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the perfect-gas T0 as the real temperature.
- Applying Newtonian theory to the leeward side (Cp ≈ 0 there).
- Using M independence below M ≈ 5.

scenes.text: A 6 mm sonic nozzle is used as a calibrated flow meter: mass flow depends only on p0 and T0.

steps.title: Aim and theory
steps.body:
**Aim**: verify ṁ = 0.0404 p0 A*/√T0 for choked flow and find the discharge coefficient C_d = ṁ_actual/ṁ_ideal.
**Apparatus**: critical-flow venturi nozzle, pressure transducer for p0, thermocouple for T0, and a reference flow meter.

steps.body:

activity.prompt: Typical viva questions with model answers.

items.q: Why does back pressure not change the mass flow once the nozzle is choked?
items.a: Information about downstream pressure cannot travel upstream through a sonic throat; the mass flux there is fixed by p0, T0 and A*.

items.q: What is the difference between stagnation and static pressure?
items.a: Stagnation pressure is the pressure if the flow were brought to rest isentropically; static pressure is what a moving fluid element feels.
One whose exit static pressure is below the ambient pressure; oblique shocks form at the exit.

items.q: Why does the shock cause loss in total pressure?
items.a: The shock is irreversible; entropy rises and p0 falls.

items.q: Why is T0 constant across a shock?
items.a: The flow is adiabatic with no work, so total enthalpy is conserved.

items.q: What is the use of a second throat in a supersonic tunnel?
items.a: It lets the starting shock be swallowed and keeps the test section supersonic while recovering pressure efficiently.

steps.title: Problem 2 – wedge (original)
steps.body:
Air at M = 3, p1 = 30 kPa, T1 = 220 K flows over a 20° wedge. Find p2, T2 and M2 (weak shock).

steps.title: Problem 3 – expansion (original)
steps.body:
Flow at M = 2, p = 80 kPa expands round a 10° convex corner. Find M2 and p2.
**Solution**: ν1 = 26.38°; ν2 = 36.38° → M2 = 2.39; p2/p1 = 0.548 → **p2 = 43.8 kPa**.

steps.title: Problem 4 – nozzle (original)
steps.body:
A rocket-test nozzle has throat area 0.02 m², exit Mach 3, p0 = 2 MPa. Find A_e and p_e.
**Solution**: A/A* = 4.235 → A_e = 0.0847 m²; p0/p = 36.73 → **p_e = 54.5 kPa**.
